title: Akiva Learns His Letters at Forty
hookLine: many adults celebrate a bar or bat mitzvah later in life
carry: torah can be learned at any age

lines: A GROWN MAN WHO CAN'T READ.
FATHER AND SON LEARN THE ALPHABET.
cards: Water drips onto a stone at the mouth of a well. Drip. Drip.
Over years it has worn a hollow into it. A man named Akiva stands looking at it. He has never learned to read, not one letter.

He's a grown man, and tradition says he's forty years old. Standing there he thinks: if soft water can carve hard stone, then surely the words of Torah, strong as iron, can carve a heart that is only flesh.
He goes home, takes his young son by the hand, and the two of them sit down with the children's teacher to learn the alphabet.

teach.b: First, Akiva, whom this path met with Rachel in year one. The well story is told in Avot de-Rabbi Natan, an early rabbinic collection.

The man who started at forty, sitting with the children over the alphabet, became, in the tradition's memory, one of its great teachers. The rabbis didn't hide his late start. They kept it in the story.
Genesis says Abraham was ninety-nine when he entered the covenant of circumcision, the covenant a baby receives at eight days old. Abraham himself came to it as an old man. Third, today.
Some adults never had a bar or bat mitzvah. Their family wasn't observant, or the ceremony wasn't offered to girls where they grew up, or life simply got in the way.

Now some synagogues run adult classes, where a group studies together, sometimes for a long stretch, and then stands up together to read from the Torah: a retired engineer learning the melody alongside a young nurse.
Fourth, what it shows. By law, a person becomes bar or bat mitzvah with age, ceremony or not. So the adult ceremony isn't a status earned late.
It's a choice made late: to stand up, to read, to teach, in front of everyone, because they want to.
Water, given time, gets through stone.

how: Some synagogues offer adult bar and bat mitzvah classes: a group studies together and then reads from the Torah together, often including people who never had the ceremony as children.

o: a promise to finish what you began as a child
starting to learn at any age, like Akiva at forty
a rule that adults must redo their coming of age

practice: Bring to mind something you once wanted to learn or do and decided you'd missed your chance at: an instrument, a language, a faith practice, a degree, a friendship you let lapse.
Picture Akiva at the well, then name the smallest first letter of that thing, the alef: one lesson, one call, one page. Hold it, and if you pray, ask for patience to begin.

wordCard.voice: Never too late. Akiva learning his letters beside his son, Abraham's covenant at ninety-nine, and adults standing up to read. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: Torah can be learned at any age. Akiva began at forty, beside his son. Until tomorrow.
